cards.back: An **interactive technology that enhances the real world by overlaying digital content** — images, animations, 3D models, contextual information — onto the user's physical surroundings **in real time**. Unlike VR, the user **remains connected to the real world**.

cards.front: The three requirements of an AR system
cards.back: **① Combines real and virtual · ② Interactive in real time · ③ Registered in 3D.** All three are required. A CGI film fails ②; a HUD fails ③. Note AR needs **no particular hardware** — audio AR qualifies.

cards.front: Why is registration the defining hard problem of AR?
cards.back: In **VR** a tracking error shifts the whole world together and often goes unnoticed. In **AR** the user sees real and virtual **simultaneously**, so misalignment shows as the virtual object **visibly sliding off** the real surface. Two error sources: **static** (miscalibration) and **dynamic** (latency).

**Real environment → Augmented Reality → Augmented Virtuality → Virtual environment.** **Mixed Reality** is everything strictly between the two extremes — so **AR is a part of MR**, not a sibling. AV = mostly virtual with real elements brought in.

**1968** Sutherland *Sword of Damocles* — first HMD · **1992** term coined by **Caudell at Boeing** — aircraft wiring · **1993** **KARMA** — industrial maintenance · **1997** **Touring Machine** — first outdoor mobile · **2003** **Invisible Trains** — handheld on PDAs · **2008** **Vuforia** — natural feature tracking on smartphones.

cards.front: The arc of AR history in one line
cards.back: **Laboratory → industrial → mobile → consumer**, driven by tracking getting cheaper and less dependent on a **prepared environment**. The 1997→2008 step is exactly **markers → natural features**.

cards.front: The five AR application domains with examples
cards.back: **Industry** — Boeing aircraft wire assembly · **Medical** — fetal imaging on the abdomen · **Navigation** — Touring Machine, modern phone/glasses apps · **Gaming** — ARQuake, Invisible Trains, Pokémon GO · **Retail** — IKEA Place.

cards.front: What do all successful AR applications have in common?
cards.back: Their value depends on virtual content being **correctly registered to a real object** — the surgeon's anatomy, the technician's cable, the customer's living room. That is why the field is dominated by tracking rather than graphics.

Technology creating **fully immersive, computer-generated environments** that **replace real-world sensory inputs**, targeting **sight, sound and sometimes touch** to induce a **sense of presence**. AR *supplements* reality; VR **fully disconnects** the user from it.

**Open loop (non-interactive)** — pre-recorded or passive; **does not respond to user input** (a 360° video). **Closed loop (interactive)** — tracks head, hands, voice and **modifies the environment in real time**. Closed-loop is what makes it VR rather than cinema — and what creates the latency problem.

**Uncanny valley** — affinity collapses when an avatar is *almost* human; a stylised avatar is often more comfortable than a nearly-photoreal one. **Motion sickness** — from **sensory discrepancy between visual motion and physical movement**; triggered by latency, artificial locomotion, low frame rate, wrong FOV/IPD.

The **psychological sensation of 'being there'**, making users perceive the virtual world as real and eliciting **genuine emotional and physical reactions**. **Example: Birdly** — simulates wind, motion and visual feedback. The test is behavioural: do they **duck**?

**Presence** (Birdly) · **Interactivity** (Half-Life: Alyx) · **First vs third person** · **Synthetic vs captured worlds** (Nimrud). Framing: **presence is the goal; the other three are the levers you pull to achieve it.**

**Synthetic** — entirely computer-generated (3D modelling); limitless creativity, full interactivity, but everything must be modelled. **Captured** — **360° video or photogrammetry** of real places; photorealistic by construction but often limited interactivity. **Trade-off: realism vs agency.**

**First person** — through the avatar's eyes; **more immersive**, higher sickness risk. **Third person** — observing your avatar; **advantageous for training and narrative storytelling**, because seeing your own posture from outside is more informative for whole-body movement.

cards.front: The four VR application domains with examples
cards.back: **Gaming** — Beat Saber · **Education** — Nimrud Palace virtual tour · **Healthcare** — surgical training, Clouds Over Sidra (empathy) · **Telepresence** — telepresence robots with panoramic video and spatial audio.

cards.front: When is AR chosen over VR?
cards.back: **AR** when the task is **anchored to a real object** and the user must stay in the real world (Boeing wiring, surgical navigation, IKEA Place). **VR** when the place or situation is **absent, dangerous or impossible** (Nimrud, surgical *simulation*, exposure therapy).

Real world seen **directly** through transparent/semi-transparent lenses with virtual content projected onto them. **Example: HoloLens.** **Pro:** zero real-world latency, natural depth, **safe on failure**. **Con:** additive only — **cannot occlude**, no true black, holograms look ghostly; narrow FOV.

**Cameras capture** the real world, it is **composited** with virtual content and shown on **internal screens**. **Example: Rift/Vive (with passthrough), Quest 3.** **Pro:** controls every pixel so virtual can **properly occlude** real. **Con:** **latency**, camera-limited resolution/FOV, **unsafe on failure**, parallax error.

Project images **directly onto physical surfaces** — **no headset**. **Example: CAVE** (Cave Automatic Virtual Environment), projecting onto the walls and floor of a room-sized cube. **Pro:** nothing worn, naturally multi-user, you see your own body. **Con:** fixed, expensive, correct from only **one tracked viewpoint**, washed out by ambient light.

**OST cannot occlude the real world but has zero real-world latency. VST can occlude but adds latency.** Everything else follows from whether light reaches the eye directly or via a camera and screen.

**World-fixed** — content anchored to the **environment**; stays put as the user moves; requires full **6DOF registration** (a hologram on a table). **User-fixed** — content anchored to the **user**; moves with them; needs little world tracking (a HUD). A HUD is **not AR** because it fails requirement ③.
**Gyroscopes** (angular rotation) + **accelerometers** (linear motion) + sometimes **magnetometers** (heading from Earth's magnetic field). 6-DOF IMU = gyro + accel; **9-DOF** = all three.

Standalone GPS: **1–100 m**; indoors it barely works. **DGPS**: a **ground station at a precisely known location** derives the current error (mostly **atmospheric**) and **broadcasts a correction** — improving accuracy to **sub-metre**. Even so, GPS is only for **coarse** localisation, never registration.

**Outside-in** — fixed external sensors watch the headset (**Lighthouse**, camera rigs); very accurate, low drift, but needs installation and confines you to a volume. **Inside-out** — the headset's own cameras watch the room (Quest, HoloLens); portable, no setup, unlimited area, but must build its own map — **SLAM**.

**High-performance GPUs** — essential for high-resolution 3D at high frame rates. **Tethered** (Rift, Vive Pro) — maximum fidelity, cable and fixed location. **Mobile/standalone** (Google Cardboard, **Meta Quest 3**) — mobile processors, portability with slightly reduced fidelity.

cards.front: Motion-to-photon latency — the budget and why
cards.back: Target **under ~20 ms** from head movement to photons reaching the eye. Why: the **vestibulo-ocular reflex** responds in **~10 ms** and is calibrated to a perfectly stable world, so any lag makes the world **swim**. This drives 90 fps, low-persistence displays and pose prediction.

**Virtual World Generator** — owns **state**: object behaviour, physics, interaction coordination. **Rendering engine** — owns **pixels**: stereoscopic rendering, real-time lighting, 60–120 fps (Unity, Unreal). **Input processing** — owns **intent**: queues, prioritises and interprets controller/hand/voice input.

cards.front: What is stereoscopic rendering and what does it cost?
cards.back: **Separate images for each eye** — two view matrices offset by the **inter-pupillary distance (IPD)**, two viewports, two projections. It is the whole Unit 2 pipeline **run twice per frame**, which is why the VR polygon budget is roughly **half** a monitor's.

cards.front: Why does consistency of frame rate matter more than height?
cards.back: A steady 72 fps is far more comfortable than a rate oscillating between 90 and 45 — **irregularity is itself a sickness trigger**. Hence **reprojection**: re-warping the last frame to the newest head pose rather than dropping a frame.

cards.front: Rods vs cones, and the fovea
cards.back: **Cones** ~6 million, concentrated in the **fovea**, sensitive to **colour and detail**. **Rods** ~120 million, in the **periphery**, sensitive to **motion and low light, no colour**. The **fovea is only ~2°** of a ~200° field, with ~1 arc-minute acuity — **you see almost nothing sharply.**

**Rapid ballistic jumps** repositioning the fovea — up to **900°/s**, 20–200 ms, **cannot be corrected mid-flight**. **Saccadic suppression:** vision is largely switched off during the jump, which is why you never see the blur. Exploited by **foveated rendering** and **redirected walking**.

**Smoothly tracks a moving target** to hold it on the fovea — works up to about **30°/s**, beyond which it breaks into catch-up saccades. **Cannot be done without a target.** It is what causes **judder** on sample-and-hold displays.

cards.front: The Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex (VOR) — and why VR cares most about it
cards.back: The eyes **counter-rotate against head movement** to hold gaze, driven by the **inner ear**, with **~10 ms latency** — faster than any visually-driven response. It is **calibrated to a perfectly stable world**, so display lag makes the image **slip across the retina** → sensory conflict → **motion sickness**. This sets the **20 ms budget**.

**OKR** tracks a **large moving visual field** (slow drift then fast reset — optokinetic nystagmus). It underlies **vection**, the illusion of self-motion — which is what makes artificial locomotion in VR feel like movement **and** what makes it nauseating.

**Vergence** — the eyes rotate in **opposite** directions (converge/diverge) to fixate at a depth; the only non-conjugate movement. **Microsaccades** — tiny involuntary tremor during fixation that **prevents perceptual fading**: a perfectly stabilised retinal image **disappears within seconds**.

Since acuity collapses outside ~2°, render **full resolution around the gaze point** and **progressively lower outside**. Saves **50–70%** of shading cost with no perceptible loss — provided the **eye tracker keeps up through a saccade**.

With **sample-and-hold**, while the eye smoothly pursues a moving object the static image **smears across the retina** (judder). Fix: illuminate each frame for only **1–2 ms**. Counter-intuitively, **the cure for blur is to show the image less** — same principle as a fast camera shutter.

In reality **vergence and focus change together**. In a headset **vergence varies** with virtual depth but **accommodation is fixed** at the screen's optical distance. Result: **eye strain, fatigue, headaches**. Proposed fixes: **varifocal**, **light-field** and **multi-focal** displays — none solved in a consumer product.

**Translation:** surge (fwd/back), sway (left/right), heave (up/down). **Rotation:** roll, pitch, yaw. **3DOF** = orientation only (Cardboard — look around but not lean). **6DOF** = adds position, needing base stations or inside-out SLAM.

cards.front: How is a pose represented mathematically?
cards.back: **$(\mathbf p, q)$** — position $\mathbf p \in \mathbb{R}^3$ plus a **unit quaternion** $q$ (no gimbal lock, compact, interpolatable). Equivalently the homogeneous matrix $T = \begin{bmatrix} R & \mathbf p \\ \mathbf 0^{\mathsf T} & 1\end{bmatrix}$ — the object's frame in world coordinates, i.e. Unit 2's **model matrix**.

**Accuracy** = closeness to the true pose. **Precision/jitter** = variation when nothing moves. A constant 2 cm offset (poor accuracy, good precision) is often unnoticeable; 2 mm of jitter (good accuracy, poor precision) makes content **visibly shake** — humans are far more sensitive to **motion** than offset.

cards.front: The tracking problem in one sentence
cards.back: **Given noisy, drifting, partially-occluded sensor readings, produce a stable 6DOF pose within 20 milliseconds.** No single sensor can; the answer is to **combine sensors so their failure modes cancel**.

**Articulated linkages** with **joint angle sensors** on a base station. **Pro:** very high precision, very low latency, reliable. **Con:** limited DOF, user **tethered to the arms**. Example: **medical simulators**. It doesn't *measure* pose — it **computes** it by forward kinematics.

A base station generates a **magnetic field**; sensors measure its **strength and orientation**. **Pro:** **no line of sight** — tracks through obstructions (hence surgical navigation). **Con:** **highly sensitive to metal and EM interference**, limited range. Example: **Polhemus**.

**Time-of-flight** of sound between transmitters and microphones. **Pro:** low cost, good in small enclosed spaces. **Con:** **noise and reflections**, limited range, line-of-sight, **slow update rate** — sound travels 343 m/s, so 3 m costs ~9 ms before any computation.

**Marker-based** — **fiducial markers** (QR-like, ARToolKit) of known geometry; high accuracy but needs line of sight, good lighting and someone to **place them**. **Markerless (NFT/SLAM)** — tracks **natural features** (corners, edges, textures); no markers, but **computationally intensive, lighting-dependent, may drift**. Example: **Vuforia, ARKit**.

cards.front: Why does a gyroscope drift? (with the maths)
cards.back: It measures **angular velocity**, so orientation requires **integration**: $\theta(t) = \theta_0 + \int\omega\,d\tau$. A constant bias $\epsilon$ gives error **$\epsilon t$ — linear in time**. A 0.01°/s bias reaches **36° after an hour**.

cards.front: Why can't an accelerometer give position?
cards.back: Position needs **double** integration, so a bias produces error $\tfrac12\epsilon t^2$ — **quadratic**. A 0.01 m/s² bias gives **18 cm after 6 seconds**, 5 m after a minute. **This is why 6DOF needs cameras or base stations.**

cards.front: What is the accelerometer actually for?
cards.back: **Measuring gravity** — an absolute reference for **roll and pitch**. It **cannot give yaw**, because rotating about the vertical axis doesn't change how gravity feels. Yaw needs a **magnetometer** (or vision).

cards.front: The complementarity that makes fusion work
cards.back: **Gyroscope** — fast and smooth, but **drifts**. **Accelerometer & magnetometer** — jittery and distortable, but **never drift**, because gravity and magnetic north don't move. **The failure modes are opposites** — the steady sensors correct the fast one's drift, the fast one smooths their jitter.

One rotational DOF, so integration is scalar addition: $\theta_{k+1} = \theta_k + \omega_k\Delta t$. With $\Delta t = 1$ s the total is just the **sum of the readings**; then rotate the point: $(1,0) \to (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. **Rotation preserves length** — a useful check.

$\Delta q = (\cos\frac{\theta}{2},\ \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot\hat{\mathbf u})$ where $\theta$ comes from **integrating angular velocity** and $\hat{\mathbf u}$ is the rotation axis. From a gyro reading: $\theta = \lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert\Delta t$ and $\hat{\mathbf u} = \boldsymbol\omega/\lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert$.

**By multiplication**, not addition: $q_{k+1} = q_k \otimes \Delta q_k$. Adding unit quaternions doesn't even give a unit quaternion. **Order encodes the frame**: $q\otimes\Delta q$ = body frame (the usual choice, since the gyro is bolted to the body); $\Delta q\otimes q$ = global frame.

① $\lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert$ = the **rate** · ② normalise for the **axis** · ③ $\theta = \lVert\boldsymbol\omega\rVert\Delta t$, then **halve it** · ④ assemble $(\cos\frac\theta2, \hat{\mathbf u}\sin\frac\theta2)$ · ⑤ **check the norm is 1**.

Integrating sensor readings forward from a known start. Works for seconds, then fails to **drift**. *Like navigating by counting steps with your eyes closed* — **you need to open your eyes occasionally**, which is what gravity and magnetic north provide.

cards.front: Why is position harder than orientation?
cards.back: Orientation has **cheap absolute references** — gravity gives down, magnetic north gives heading. **Position has none**; nothing you can feel tells you where you are. So position needs an **external reference**: cameras, base stations or GPS. Hence 3DOF is cheap and 6DOF is not.

**Outside-in optical** (Lighthouse, mocap) · **inside-out optical / SLAM** (Quest, HoloLens, ARKit) · **marker-based** (ARToolKit) · **GPS** (outdoor, coarse) · **ultrasonic/EM**. All answer *'where am I relative to something that doesn't move?'* — combined with the IMU, which fills gaps at high rate.

cards.front: Tracking attached bodies — the kinematic chain
cards.back: A chain of rigid bodies with each pose **relative to its parent** — Unit 1's frame hierarchy, Unit 2's scene graph. World pose = **concatenation of every transform from the root**. Benefits: **fewer parameters, physically plausible results, robust to occlusion**. *The skeleton is a prior.*

**FK**: joint angles → end-effector position; straightforward concatenation (Unit 1's arm question). **IK**: desired end-effector pose → joint angles; **may have many solutions or none**. VR avatar animation is **IK** — the system knows only head and two hands, which is why VR elbows often look wrong.

**Gradual accumulation of error over time** in estimated position/orientation. Causes: **sensor bias** (a constant offset) and **numerical integration errors**. Symptom: content **slowly wandering** from its anchor. Fixed by **sensor fusion**, not filtering.

**Random fluctuations** in sensor measurements from **electronic interference, temperature variations, mechanical vibrations**. Symptom: content **shaking or jittering** in place — e.g. an accelerometer reading changes while the device is stationary. Fixed by **filtering**.

**You cannot filter away drift and you cannot fuse away noise.** Drift is **systematic and accumulates** — averaging a bias gives you the bias; it needs an **absolute reference**. Noise is **random and zero-mean** — it **does** average out, so it needs **smoothing over time**.

An **optimal recursive filter** minimising **mean squared error**, combining prior estimates with new measurements while **modelling noise explicitly**. Two steps: **predict** (forecast from a motion model, grow uncertainty) then **update** (blend with measurement, shrink uncertainty). 'Optimal' holds for **linear + Gaussian**; real systems use EKF/UKF.

$\theta_{k+1} = \alpha(\theta_k + \omega\Delta t) + (1-\alpha)\theta_{\text{accel}}$, with $\alpha \approx 0.95$–$0.98$. A **high-pass on the gyro** and a **low-pass on the accelerometer** — each sensor used only where it's good. Cheap, one parameter, no covariance matrices.

cards.front: Tilt drift vs heading drift — which sensor corrects each?
cards.back: **Tilt drift** (roll & pitch) ← **accelerometer**, which measures **gravity**. **Heading drift** (yaw) ← **magnetometer**, which measures **magnetic north**. The accelerometer **cannot** fix yaw. Corrections are applied as a **small fraction each step**, because the accelerometer is only valid when the device isn't accelerating.

cards.front: Define sensor fusion and why it is needed
cards.back: **Intelligently combining data from multiple sensors** to produce more accurate, reliable tracking than any one alone. Needed because **gyros drift**, **accelerometers are motion-sensitive and noisy**, and **magnetometers are distorted by metal** — but their weaknesses are **complementary**.

**① Normalize** accelerometer + magnetometer to unit length (only direction matters) · **② derive roll, pitch, yaw** — an absolute reference (accel→roll/pitch, mag→yaw) · **③ convert to quaternions and combine with gyro $\Delta q$** — fast response + long-term stability · **④ re-normalize** to stop floating-point error accumulating.

cards.front: Why convert to quaternions in step 3?
cards.back: Euler angles are convenient to **compute** from gravity and north but suffer **gimbal lock** and blend badly. Once both estimates are quaternions they combine smoothly with no singularities. **Euler is the input format; quaternion is the working format.**

**AR/VR headsets** (Quest, Vive, HoloLens) — smooth head tracking, realistic alignment of virtual with physical, **minimised motion sickness**. **Robotics** — drones and autonomous vehicles fusing **IMU + GPS + LIDAR + cameras** for navigation in cluttered or GPS-denied environments. Same architecture, different scale.
